title: Make String Anti-palindrome
statement:
A string of even length `n` is an **anti-palindrome** when no character equals its mirror: `s[i] != s[n - 1 - i]` for every `0 <= i < n`.

You are given a string `s` of even length. You may swap any two of its characters, as many times as you like (zero swaps is fine), so any rearrangement of `s` can be reached. Return the lexicographically smallest anti-palindrome that can be produced this way. If no rearrangement of `s` is an anti-palindrome, return the string `"-1"`.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Any sequence of swaps can reach any rearrangement, so the task is to pick the smallest rearrangement whose mirrored pairs all differ. Trying every rearrangement is factorial. Instead, notice that the smallest possible first half is the `n / 2` smallest letters in sorted order, and a valid answer with that first half exists whenever any answer exists. After sorting, the only letter that can clash with its mirror is the one sitting on both sides of the middle; pushing the smallest larger letters into the clashing spots fixes it while keeping the string as small as possible.

## Approach

1. Sort the characters into `chars` and let `half = n / 2`.
2. If `chars[half]` differs from `chars[half - 1]`, every second-half letter is bigger than its mirror, so the sorted string is the answer.
3. Otherwise call that shared letter `middle` and move `next` past its run in the second half to the first bigger letter.
4. Walk `j` from `half` while `chars[j]` equals its mirror `chars[n - 1 - j]`. Swap `chars[j]` with `chars[next]` and advance `next`.
5. If a clash remains but `next` has reached `n`, there are not enough other letters: return `"-1"`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "abca"` sorts to `chars = ['a', 'a', 'b', 'c']` with `half = 2`. `chars[2] = 'b'` and `chars[1] = 'a'` differ, so no pair clashes and the answer is `"aabc"`. (In Example 3, `"cccd"` sorts to `"cccd"`; the first clash at `j = 2` swaps in the `d`, the second clash at `j = 3` finds `next = 4 = n`, so the answer is `"-1"`.)

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the fix-up loop is O(n). A counting sort would make it O(n).
- Space: O(n) for the character array.

## Pitfalls

- Return the string `"-1"`, not the number.
- Repair clashes in the second half only; touching the sorted first half would make the string bigger.
- The impossible case is a letter appearing more than `n / 2` times; the loop detects it when `next` runs off the end.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `chars` | the sorted characters, repaired in place |
| `half` | index where the second half starts |
| `middle` | the letter on both sides of the middle when they clash |
| `next` | next bigger letter in the second half to swap in |
| `j` | second-half position being checked against its mirror |

narration.2: Sort the characters: the first half is now the smallest possible first half.
narration.4: The second half starts at index half.
narration.5: If the two middle letters differ, every second-half letter is bigger than its mirror.
narration.6: So the sorted string is already the smallest anti-palindrome.
narration.8: Otherwise remember the letter that sits on both sides of the middle.
narration.10: Skip the run of that letter at the start of the second half.
narration.13: Walk the second half while a letter equals its mirror.
narration.14: No bigger letter is left to swap in...
narration.15: ...so some letter appears more than n / 2 times and no answer exists.
narration.17: Swap the smallest unused bigger letter into the clashing spot.
narration.18: The next swap uses the following letter.
narration.20: All clashes are fixed; join the characters into the answer.
